pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans and related Xanthomonas species
summary: A bacterial disease that spots leaves, stems and green fruit. Infected leaves stay on the plant and turn yellow and ragged.
symptoms: Small (under 3 mm) dark, greasy or water-soaked spots, sometimes with a yellow halo
Spot centres may fall out, making leaves ragged
Raised, scabby spots on green fruit
key_sign: Small dark greasy spots with yellowing; no rings and no grey centres.
favourable_conditions: Warm, wet weather with wind-driven rain or overhead irrigation.
spread: Carried on seed and transplants; spreads by splashing water, hands and tools.

today: Remove badly spotted leaves; avoid working among wet plants
this_week: Apply copper plus mancozeb, as registered, before rain
Switch to drip irrigation or water at the base
next_two_weeks: Repeat at label intervals while it stays wet

chemical: Copper plus mancozeb alternated with acibenzolar-S-methyl, where registered. Copper-resistant strains are common, so do not rely on copper alone
cultural: Rotate away from tomato and pepper for 2-3 years

prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants

sources.title: Clemson Extension: Controlling bacterial spot on tomato and pepper
University of Minnesota Extension: Tomato leaf spot diseases

summary: A very common fungal disease. Target-like spots start on the oldest leaves and move up; plants can lose many leaves but often still fruit.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (bull's-eye) and a yellow margin
Starts on the lowest, oldest leaves
Dark leathery spots near the stem end of fruit
key_sign: Brown spots with concentric rings like a target, on the lowest leaves first.
favourable_conditions: Warm, humid weather with alternating wet and dry periods.
spread: Survives in infected debris, soil and on seed; spreads by rain splash and wind.

today: Pinch off spotted lower leaves (removing up to a third of the leaves is fine early on)
Mulch the soil to stop spores splashing up
this_week: If spots keep spreading, apply a fungicide registered for early blight
Stake or cage plants and prune the lowest leaves for airflow
next_two_weeks: Repeat protection at label intervals in humid weather
Keep plants well fed and evenly watered

chemical: Mancozeb, chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin, or azoxystrobin + difenoconazole, as registered; rotate groups
organic: Copper fungicides; Bacillus subtilis-based biofungicides; seed treatment with Trichoderma
cultural: Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest

TNAU Agritech: Tomato early blight

summary: A fast, destructive disease that can kill tomato plants within days in cool, wet weather. The same pathogen attacks potato.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked patches that turn olive then brown
White, downy growth under the leaf in humid conditions
Brown lesions on stems and petioles
Firm, greasy brown blotches on fruit
key_sign: Fast-spreading, water-soaked patches with white fuzz underneath in humid weather.
favourable_conditions: Cool nights (about 10-20 °C), mild days, and long wet periods from rain, fog or dew.
spread: Wind-blown spores travel long distances; also spread by infected transplants and potato tubers.

today: Remove and bag infected plants; do not compost them
Tell nearby tomato and potato growers
this_week: Protect remaining plants immediately with a fungicide registered for late blight, then at short label intervals
Avoid overhead watering and keep foliage dry
next_two_weeks: Keep spraying while cool, wet weather continues
Destroy all infected material at the end of the season

chemical: Mancozeb, chlorothalonil, cyazofamid, azoxystrobin or other late-blight products as registered; rotate groups

prevention: Never plant near cull potato piles

sources.title: TNAU Agritech: Tomato late blight
UMass Extension: Tomato leaf blights

summary: A fungus that thrives in humid greenhouses and dense plantings. Pale spots on top of leaves match velvety olive mould underneath.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to greyish-brown velvety mould directly beneath
Leaves curl, wither and drop
key_sign: Yellow spots on top with olive velvety mould on the underside.
favourable_conditions: Relative humidity above about 85% with poor airflow; very common in polyhouses and greenhouses.
spread: Spores spread by air, tools and clothing; survives on debris and greenhouse structures.

today: Remove infected leaves and carry them out in a bag
this_week: Reduce humidity: ventilate, space plants, prune lower leaves, and water in the morning
Apply a fungicide registered for leaf mould if it keeps spreading
next_two_weeks: Keep humidity down; check the undersides of new leaves

chemical: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb or other fungicides labelled for tomato leaf mould
cultural: Ventilate and heat greenhouses to stop condensation
Clean and disinfect the structure between crops

sources.title: UConn IPM: Vegetable pest message (spider mites, leaf mold)
UMass Extension: Tomato leaf blights

summary: One of the most destructive tomato leaf diseases. Many small spots appear on lower leaves after fruit set and can strip plants of foliage.
symptoms: Many small (2-3 mm) round spots with grey-white centres and dark borders
Tiny black dots inside spot centres (seen with a magnifier)
Starts on lower leaves after fruit set; leaves yellow and fall
key_sign: Many small round spots with pale grey centres and dark borders.
favourable_conditions: Warm, wet weather and leaf wetness; splashing from soil.
spread: Survives on crop debris and related weeds; spores splash from soil and lower leaves.

this_week: Apply a fungicide registered for Septoria leaf spot if spots move up the plant
Water at the base early in the day
next_two_weeks: Repeat at label intervals during wet weather

chemical: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb or other fungicides labelled for Septoria
cultural: Rotate away from tomato for at least 1-2 years
Remove plant debris at season end

prevention: Stake plants and keep lower leaves off the soil
Most varieties are susceptible, so prevention matters

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Tomato leaf spot diseases

summary: Not a disease but a tiny pest. Mites suck sap from the underside of leaves, causing fine speckling, bronzing and webbing in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckles (stippling) on the upper leaf
Fine silk webbing under leaves and between stems
Leaves turn bronze, dry and drop
key_sign: Fine pale speckling with tiny moving dots and webbing underneath.
favourable_conditions: Hot, dry, dusty conditions; populations explode quickly in warm weather and greenhouses.
spread: Mites crawl between touching plants and are carried by wind, clothing and tools.

today: Confirm: tap a leaf over white paper and look for moving specks
Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water
this_week: If numbers are high, apply a miticide or horticultural oil registered for tomato, covering leaf undersides
next_two_weeks: Re-check after a week; repeat treatments as per label, rotating products

chemical: Miticides registered for tomato (for example abamectin, where permitted); rotate modes of action
organic: Insecticidal soap, neem or horticultural oils; release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
cultural: Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators

prevention: Scout leaf undersides weekly in hot, dry weather

sources.title: UMass Extension: Two-spotted spider mite
UConn IPM: Vegetable pest message (spider mites, leaf mold)

summary: A fungal disease of warm, humid regions that causes ringed leaf spots, heavy leaf drop inside the canopy and pitted fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with light-brown centres and faint concentric rings
Spots start on older leaves inside the canopy
Pitted, sunken spots on fruit
key_sign: Ringed brown spots similar to early blight, often without the yellow halo.
favourable_conditions: Moderate to warm temperatures (about 21-27 °C) with high humidity and dense canopies.
spread: Spores spread by wind and rain; the fungus has a wide host range and survives on debris.

today: Remove spotted leaves from the inner canopy
this_week: Open the canopy by pruning and staking
Apply a fungicide registered for target spot if it spreads
next_two_weeks: Repeat protection at label intervals in humid weather

chemical: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin or other products labelled for target spot; rotate groups
cultural: Prune for airflow; avoid excess nitrogen

prevention: Scout inside the canopy, not just outer leaves

pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (spread by whitefly Bemisia tabaci)
summary: A whitefly-spread virus with no cure. Infected young plants become stunted and produce little or no fruit.
symptoms: Young leaves small, cupped upward, with yellow edges
Plants stunted and bushy
Flowers drop; very little fruit set
key_sign: Small, upward-curled young leaves with yellow margins on a stunted plant.
favourable_conditions: Hot weather with high whitefly populations.
spread: Spread only by whiteflies and infected transplants; not spread by touch or seed.

today: Remove infected plants (bag them first so whiteflies do not fly off)
this_week: Install yellow sticky traps and control whiteflies with registered products
Protect nurseries and young plants with insect-proof netting
next_two_weeks: Control weed hosts around the field

chemical: No cure for the virus. Control the whitefly vector with insecticides registered for tomato (for example thiamethoxam or imidacloprid where permitted), rotating modes of action
organic: Neem oil or insecticidal soap against whiteflies; reflective (silver) mulches
cultural: Grow barrier crops such as maize or sorghum around the field

prevention: Leave a tomato-free period between crops to break the cycle

TNAU Agritech: Tomato leaf curl virus

summary: A very stable virus spread by touch, tools and seed. There is no cure; infected plants yield less, lower-quality fruit.
symptoms: Light- and dark-green mottled (mosaic) leaves
Distorted, fern-like or narrow leaves
Uneven ripening or internal browning of fruit
key_sign: Light-and-dark green mosaic mottling with distorted leaves.
favourable_conditions: Any conditions; spread is driven by handling plants.
spread: Spreads on hands, tools, clothing and infected seed; survives for long periods in debris and on surfaces.

today: Wash hands with soap before touching healthy plants
this_week: Disinfect tools, stakes and trays (for example with a 10% bleach solution or a skim-milk dip during work)
Do not smoke or handle tobacco near plants
next_two_weeks: Watch neighbouring plants for new mottling
Do not save seed from infected plants

organic: No organic cure; strict hygiene is the only control
cultural: Clean tools and hands between plants

prevention: Plant resistant varieties (Tm-2 or Tm-2² genes)

summary: No disease signs were found on this tomato leaf.
symptoms: Even green colour
No spots, powder or distortion
key_sign: Uniform green leaf with no spots.

this_week: Inspect a few plants, including leaf undersides
next_two_weeks: Keep monitoring, especially after rain or humid spells

prevention: Water at the base in the morning
